conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m <med>Dr. Maya Bennett</med>, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My role is to check in on how moms are feeling in the weeks and months after birth, because the emotional changes that come with new motherhood are just as important as the physical ones.

Today I’ll be using a quick screening tool called the <med>Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale</med>, or EPDS. It’s a set of 10 questions about mood, anxiety, and coping over the past seven days. It isn’t a test of “good” or “bad” parenting—just a way to see how you’re really doing so we can offer the right support.

Everything you share is confidential; the only exception is if you tell me you might harm yourself or someone else—in that case we’d talk together about immediate safety. We’ll take one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words. We’ll keep it conversational and relaxed.

Ready to begin? 

Thinking about the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[soft half-smile, then sigh]

Honestly… not very often. I *want* to—my husband will make a joke or the baby will make a silly face—but most of the time it just feels flat, like I’m too tired or distracted to really find it funny. Maybe once or twice this week I actually laughed out loud, and even then it faded pretty fast.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, I’ll smile if someone else is laughing, but it feels forced. Most of the week I’ve just felt too worn-out or worried about the baby to find anything genuinely funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[slow shrug]

I try to. I’ll tell myself, “Tomorrow we’ll go for a walk” or “I’ll make that coffee I used to love,” but when the moment comes it feels… meh. Like the color’s drained out of it. I still go, because I know I should, yet the little spark I used to feel—anticipating my favorite show or even just a quiet shower—barely shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah… Like, if the baby won’t settle, I’ll catch myself thinking, “You must be doing something wrong—other moms seem to manage.” It’s not constant, but a couple of nights this week, when he kept crying even after I fed and changed him, I lay there wondering what I was missing, if I’d already messed up somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… I’ll be sitting there, baby’s breathing fine, nothing’s actually wrong, but my chest feels tight anyway. I keep checking the monitor, thinking maybe he stopped breathing, or I’ll suddenly worry that a car backfiring outside woke him up. There isn’t a real reason, but the feeling just barges in.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[wrapping cardigan tighter around myself]

A couple of times. Yesterday afternoon the baby was napping and I was folding laundry—totally normal moment—but suddenly my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn’t get a deep breath. There wasn’t anything happening, no noise or anything, but I had to sit down and keep telling myself, “He’s okay, you’re okay.” It passed after a minute, but it left me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days. Between feeding every few hours, trying to nap when I can, the constant laundry, texts from family asking for pictures—somehow it all feels like too much. I’ll start one chore, the baby cries, and suddenly I’m near tears because I can’t even finish folding a tiny onesie. I’m keeping up, but only just barely, and it feels like I’m always one step away from everything toppling over.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly “unhappy” in a big, hopeless way… but my brain won’t turn off. I’ll lie there exhausted, thinking about the next feed, or replaying every little sound the baby made, and sleep just slips away. It’s happened maybe three or four nights this week—takes me an hour or more to drift off, then I jolt awake at every tiny grunt from the crib.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes… I wouldn’t call it all-day despair, but there’s this dull ache that shows up most evenings. I’ll be rocking the baby, everything technically fine, and I just feel… heavy. I cried once, on Thursday night, when my husband asked how my day was—couldn’t even explain why, just felt suddenly miserable. It usually lifts after a while, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not quite that extreme. I’ve cried—once this week, maybe twice—but it wasn’t this constant, can’t-stop sort of thing. It was more like a sudden wave that came and went, and then I just felt empty and tired.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—never. I get tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again and be able to take care of my baby.

You've shared that the past week has felt flat and heavy-laughter rarely comes, simple pleasures feel colorless, and each evening brings a dull ache you can't quite explain. Despite loving your baby and keeping up appearances, you're running on empty, bombarded by racing thoughts and sudden waves of panic, and you feel one tiny setback away from everything crashing down.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 20, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes inability to find things funny, only forcing smiles, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes markedly blunted anticipation and enjoyment, clearly "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a couple of nights this week" when the baby won’t settle, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries without real triggers and persistent physical anxiety, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden racing heart and breathlessness with no trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, tearfulness, and feeling on the verge of collapse, aligning with 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, sleep-disrupting rumination and hyper-vigilance about the baby, occurring on 3–4 nights this week, which aligns with "Yes, sometimes" in the context of unhappiness-related insomnia.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent but not constant sadness: a recurring "dull ache" most evenings and at least one unprovoked crying episode within the week, aligning with "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 20/30, well above the ≥14 cutoff, indicates probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset. Items map to <med>DSM-5 criteria</med>: depressed mood most days (<sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>crying</sym>), markedly diminished interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), fatigue, guilt, concentration worries, and anxiety. No self-harm ideation (Q10=0). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> for full evaluation
2. Ask about <med>counseling</med> or <med>CBT</med> and consider <med>medication discussion</med> if symptoms persist
3. Contact <med>Postpartum Support International</med> warm-line 1-800-944-4773 or text 800-944-4773 (English & Spanish) for 24/7 support
4. Schedule brief daily check-ins with partner/friend to share mood and reduce isolation
5. Practice 10-minute wind-down routine (dim lights, no screens, slow breathing) to ease <sym>insomnia</sym>
6. Re-screen EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress and adjust care plan
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 20: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (within first 12 weeks). Source: self-report via EPDS-style questionnaire.

Primary symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, “heavy” feelings most evenings  
- Marked loss of enjoyment / anticipatory pleasure (anhedonia)  
- Episodic tearfulness (1–2×/week)  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt regarding infant care  
- Free-floating anxiety with physical symptoms (chest tightness, racing heart)  
- Two sudden panic-like episodes (no trigger)  
- Sleep-onset insomnia linked to intrusive worries about infant safety  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed and “one step away from toppling”

Pattern  
Symptoms present most days for ≥2 weeks; worse in evenings; no current suicidal ideation.

Risk indicators  
- Meets threshold items for possible minor-moderate depressive episode and comorbid anxiety  
- Functional impact: difficulty completing household tasks, impaired ability to relax when infant sleeps  
- Protective factors: denies self-harm ideation, motivated to feel better and care for baby

Screening conclusion  
Elevated score range consistent with likely postpartum depression with prominent anxiety features.  
Safety: no self-harm reported; continue routine safety inquiry at each contact.  
Recommendation: refer for comprehensive clinical assessment to determine diagnosis and appropriate level of care.
